concepts.def: The US advanced-manufacturing production credit: a per-unit federal tax credit for domestically made battery cells, modules, and components — the incentive pulling battery manufacturing onshore.

The highest transmission voltage in common use in the United States. A 765 kV line carries several times the power of a 345 kV line on one right-of-way with lower losses, which is why it is the backbone choice when a region must move gigawatts across hundreds of miles. AEP built and operates most of the country's existing 765 kV network; Texas chose it in 2025 for the Permian Basin plan.

The next-generation data-center power architecture: distributing 800-volt direct current to the rack instead of low-voltage AC. Higher voltage means lower current and losses, fewer conversion stages, and far less copper for megawatt-class racks.

Anti-dumping and countervailing duties: US trade remedies against imports priced below fair value or subsidized at home. Even a petition creates pricing risk, because duties can apply retroactively to goods already entered.

A power-generation gas turbine derived from an aircraft engine rather than designed as a heavy industrial frame. Lighter and far quicker to start than a heavy-duty machine, in blocks of roughly tens of megawatts — and because the cores can come from retiring airliners, sourceable outside the heavy-frame factory queue that sets everyone else's delivery date.

Allowance for funds used during construction: the financing cost a utility is allowed to add to the price of a plant while it is being built, so the plant enters rate base at construction cost plus the interest and equity return accrued during the build. It is a non-cash earning until the plant enters service.
aliases: allowance for funds used during construction

concepts.def: The authorization from a state or local air agency that a combustion source needs before it can be built and run, written around what leaves the stack — chiefly nitrogen oxides and particulates — and around how many hours it may run. For an on-site power plant it is usually the longest lead item after the machines themselves, and its terms decide whether the same engine may be used as backup only or as prime power.

The return on equity a commission authorizes a utility to earn on its rate base — typically nine to ten percent in recent US decisions. Because it multiplies every dollar of plant, a tenth of a point moves tens of millions a year on a large utility, which is why the return is the most litigated number in a rate case.

The explosive release of energy when current jumps through the air between conductors — a blast hot enough to be lethal at a panel door. An arc-flash study calculates that energy at every piece of gear so the right protective clothing and breaker settings can be specified, and it has to be redone whenever the electrical system changes.

Automatic transfer switch: the device that senses utility failure, signals the generators to start, and moves the load onto them once generation is stable — then manages the return trip when utility power comes back. It is the conductor of a data center's outage choreography.
Adding new battery capacity to an operating storage plant to offset degradation, keeping the plant at its contracted capacity over its life.

How long a UPS can carry its rated load from stored energy alone — seconds for a flywheel, minutes for a battery string. It is sized to cover the generator's start with a margin, not to run the hall: a longer autonomy is insurance against the engine failing its first start attempt, and it is bought in battery cabinets and floor space.

A contracted promise about the fraction of hours a plant will be ready to perform, with money attached to missing it. It matters more than an average suggests, because storage and generation revenue concentrate into a small number of extreme-price hours — a site that is available almost all year and unavailable for the wrong afternoon has not lost a proportional share of its income.

The entity that keeps generation and load matched second by second inside a defined area of the grid. In an RTO region the RTO is the balancing authority; outside one, a large vertically integrated utility can be its own — it dispatches its own plants, holds its own reserves and has no organized capacity market to buy from.

Whether lenders and investors will finance a project or accept a supplier — a function of certifications, warranties, balance-sheet strength, track record, and policy exposure rather than spec-sheet performance.

Studying a group of interconnection requests together rather than one at a time, so the effect of all of them on the same corridor is modelled at once. ERCOT proposed batching large-load requests in 2025 after serial studies could not keep up; the price is that every request in the batch waits for the slowest.

Battery backup unit: a small battery shelf inside the rack itself, carrying the servers for seconds rather than minutes — long enough to cover a transfer or ride out a disturbance. It moves the last line of stored energy from the UPS room to the point of use.

Generation or storage connected on the customer's side of the utility meter, serving the site directly — like on-site power at a data-center campus — versus front-of-the-meter assets selling into the grid.

Battery energy storage system: a grid-connected battery plant — cells packaged into modules and enclosures plus power conversion, thermal management, and controls. Rated in MW (power) and MWh (energy).

Restarting a dead network with no outside power to draw on: small units boot first to energize controls and fuel systems, then larger machines and load return in stages. Rarely exercised on the grid and definitional for an island or a microgrid, which has nothing else to start from.

The share of a generator's rating that can be applied in a single step without voltage and frequency sagging past what the load tolerates. A set that accepts 100 percent block load can pick up a whole data hall at once; one that cannot must have the load added in stages by the transfer or paralleling controls.

Battery management system: the electronics that watch every cell's voltage, current, and temperature, balance the cells, and disconnect the battery when limits are crossed — the battery's safety and health guardian.

On-site generation installed to carry a campus through the years before its grid connection matures, after which the site converts to grid supply and the same plant becomes its backup. The gear and the permits are typically sized for a run of a few years, so the contract is temporary even when the machines are not.

A site that already carries industrial infrastructure — most valuably an existing grid connection and substation from a retired plant. In a market where interconnection is the long pole, inheriting energized wires can move a project years ahead of an equivalent greenfield, which is why retired coal and industrial sites are being bought for their electrical position rather than their land.

The workhorse step-down switching converter: a switch chops the input on and off thousands to millions of times a second, and an inductor and capacitor smooth the chopped pulses into a lower steady voltage set by the fraction of time the switch is on. Several bucks running out of step with each other — a multiphase buck — share the current and cancel each other's ripple, which is how the regulators beside a processor deliver hundreds of amps.

A procurement structure in which a developer builds a generation or storage project and then transfers ownership to the utility at commercial operation. It gives the utility rate-based ownership without carrying construction risk, and gives the developer a defined exit. The middle option between a purchase agreement, where the utility never owns the asset, and a self-build, where it carries every risk.

A DC-DC stage that steps a distribution voltage down by a fixed ratio, like a transformer for direct current, without trying to hold its output constant. Giving up regulation lets it run at its resonant sweet spot with very high efficiency and density; a separate regulator elsewhere in the chain does the holding.

A solid bar of copper or aluminum used instead of cable to carry very large currents over short distances inside equipment, a rack, or a switchboard. It is the same idea as facility busway one scale smaller and inside the machine, and its cross-section is the only thing standing between the current and the heat that current makes.

Prefabricated bus bar running overhead along a row of racks, with tap-off boxes that branch power down to each cabinet. It replaces bundles of individually pulled feeders, so capacity can be added or moved without rewiring — which is why the 800 VDC designs distribute at the row on busway rather than conduit.
How fast a battery charges or discharges relative to its capacity: 1C empties it in one hour, 0.25C in four. Grid storage typically runs at low C-rates — multi-hour durations rather than sprints.

The energy a plant actually produced over a period divided by what it would have produced running flat out the whole time. A nuclear unit near 90 percent runs almost continuously; a solar farm in the 20s runs only when the sun does; a peaker in single digits runs only on the hardest days.

A market that pays a resource for being available to serve peak demand — a payment for existing, not for energy produced. PJM runs its auction, the Base Residual Auction, three years ahead; the clearing price per megawatt-day is the signal that new data-center load has moved the region from surplus to scarcity, and it flows straight into a regulated utility's bills.

Certificate of convenience and necessity: Texas's name for the commission order that lets a utility build a specific line or, outside ERCOT, a plant. In ERCOT it is issued for transmission — a wires-only utility's CCN case decides the route and the need for a 345 kV or 765 kV line, never a generator.

Coolant distribution unit: the heat exchanger and pump station that separates the facility's water loop from the clean liquid loop feeding the servers, delivering coolant to the cold plates at the right temperature and pressure. It is the interface that lets one facility cooling spine serve many different rack designs.

Arkansas's certificate of environmental compatibility and public need — the state's version of a CPCN, the commission order a utility must obtain before building a major generating plant or transmission line and putting it in rate base.
aliases: certificate of environmental compatibility and public need

concepts.def: Minnesota's version of the certificate: the commission's finding that a specific large plant or line is needed, issued in its own docket after the resource plan has set the direction. A combustion turbine or a transmission line in Minnesota needs one before it can be built and recovered.

A transfer that closes onto the new source before opening the old one, so the two are briefly in parallel and the load never sees a break. It requires the generator to be synchronized to the utility first, and the utility's permission, because for a fraction of a second the site's engines are feeding the grid.

A customer's demand at the moment the whole system peaks, as opposed to its own highest hour. Transmission and capacity costs are allocated on it, so a flat load such as a data center that draws the same at the system peak as at 3 a.m. is charged a full share — and a load that can back off for the peak hours can shed a large part of its bill.

A liquid-cooled metal block clamped directly onto a processor, carrying heat away in a coolant loop instead of an air stream. Above roughly 100 kW per rack air physically cannot move the heat fast enough, so liquid has to touch the silicon.
Data-center space, power, and cooling leased to tenants who bring their own IT equipment. Colocation providers are the landlords of the AI buildout.

Two heat engines on one fuel: a gas turbine burns the gas, and its hot exhaust then boils water to spin a second, steam turbine. Recovering that otherwise-wasted heat pushes modern plants past 60 percent efficiency — the highest of any gas machine — at the cost of far more equipment and a much longer build than simple cycle.

The structured testing that proves a finished plant performs as contracted before it is handed over and paid for. For storage it is where capacity and round-trip-efficiency guarantees are measured; for a data center it is where the outage choreography gets rehearsed rather than discovered in production.

The property that any single component can be taken out of service for planned work without dropping the critical load — the defining requirement of Uptime Tier III. It is decided by topology rather than by equipment quality: there must be a second path, and the switch onto it must itself be safe.

A recurring commission review of a certified project while it is being built — schedule, spend against the certified cost, and whether the money so far was prudent — so cost overruns are examined as they happen rather than in one prudence review at the end. Georgia adopted it for Vogtle 3 and 4.

The generator rating for carrying a constant load at full output for unlimited hours a year, as a power station would. It is the most conservative of the standard ratings — the same engine carries a smaller number as continuous than as prime or standby — and the one a permanently islanded campus should be reading.

Output power divided by input power for a converter — the rest leaves as heat. Efficiency is a curve, not a number: it collapses at light load and peaks somewhere below full load, so where a unit is parked on that curve matters as much as its headline figure.

One place in a power chain where electricity changes form or level — AC to DC, one DC voltage to another, one AC voltage to another. Each stage costs roughly one to three percent of the power as heat that must then be cooled, plus a box, floor space, and a way to fail; designing a power architecture is largely the art of deleting stages.

The question of who pays for a shared upgrade — the customer whose request triggered it, everyone in the rate class, or every ratepayer. Cost-causation says whoever causes the cost pays it; socialization spreads it. Large-load tariffs, contribution-in-aid-of-construction rules and transmission cost allocation are all answers to the same question.

A ceiling on what a utility may recover from customers for a certified project. Costs above the cap fall on shareholders unless the commission later finds them prudent, which is why a certified cost figure matters as much to the utility as the approval itself.

The ratemaking method behind almost every US regulated utility: customers pay the utility's prudent costs of serving them — operations, fuel, depreciation, taxes — plus a return on the rate base. Rates are set by customer class, so the cost-of-service study is where the argument over who pays for a data center's substation is actually fought.

A large iron-cored inductor placed in series between the utility and a rotary UPS's synchronous machine, or between the units of an isolated-parallel bus. Because an inductor resists sudden changes in current, it lets the machine hold its output voltage clean while the supply behind it dips, distorts or fails, and it limits how much of a fault on one side is felt on the other.

Certificate of public convenience and necessity: the commission's permission to build a specific plant or line and put it into rate base. An IRP says what a utility expects to need; a CPCN is the docket in which it proves one project is needed, prudent and the right choice — and the order that turns a plan into a purchase.
aliases: certificate of public convenience and necessity

concepts.def: The collateral a utility requires from a large new customer before it builds for it — a letter of credit, a cash deposit, a parent-company guaranty or a surety bond — sized to some months or years of the minimum bill, so that a customer that walks away leaves money behind rather than a stranded substation.

When one customer class pays part of the cost of serving another. The live version: whether residential bills rise to pay for the generation and wires a data-center cluster requires — the finding regulators, legislatures and state auditors have been testing, and the political reason large-load tariffs exist.

Common Redundant Power Supply: the industry-standard shape, connector, and signaling for a server power-supply module, so any compliant vendor's unit fits any compliant server. Standardizing the slot is what turns server power into a contested commodity market rather than a per-vendor design.

How much current a converter or conductor delivers per unit of area, usually amps per square centimetre of board or package footprint. As chip currents climb past a thousand amps, the current density a regulator can achieve decides whether it fits beside — or beneath — the processor at all.

A converter that trades voltage for current at a fixed ratio — halve the voltage, double the current — much as a gear train trades speed for torque. In a factorized power chain it is the stage nearest the load, turning a modest current at a higher voltage into the very large current the chip needs at about one volt.

Making several converters or supplies that feed one bus each carry a fair fraction of the load instead of one hogging it. Without deliberate sharing, small differences in output voltage let one unit take everything and overheat while its neighbours idle.

Being instructed to reduce output or consumption because the network cannot accommodate it at that moment. For a generator it is power that cannot be sold; for a very large load it is a contractual duty to back off — and a curtailment protocol is the document saying under what conditions, for how long, and who decides.

Construction work in progress: plant that is being built but is not yet in service. Normally it earns no return until it is finished; a legislature or commission that lets CWIP into rate base lets the utility charge customers for a plant before it produces anything, which lowers financing cost and shifts construction risk toward customers.

How many full charge-discharge cycles a cell delivers before its capacity falls to a stated fraction of new — commonly 70 or 80 percent. It is the number a storage warranty is written around, and it is quoted against specific depth-of-discharge and temperature conditions, so two figures are only comparable when those conditions match.

A converter that changes one DC voltage to another without passing through AC. It is the stage that does the work once power has arrived as direct current — inside a rack, inside a vehicle, or on a server board — and it is what lets a high-voltage DC bus feed low-voltage electronics.

The direct-current stage inside a static UPS between the rectifier and the inverter, where the battery connects. Every watt the load draws in double conversion passes through it as DC, which is why the batteries can take over without any switching event — they are already on the bus.

Distribution cost recovery factor: a Texas rider that lets a wires utility recover new distribution investment between base rate cases, filed annually against a statutory formula. With interim transmission updates it is the reason a Texas TDU's earnings track its capital plan with only months of lag rather than years.

A rate mechanism that separates a utility's revenue from the volume of energy it sells, so that selling less does not cut its earnings and selling more does not raise them — with a true-up each year. It removes the utility's incentive to oppose efficiency, and it changes what data-center load growth is worth to it: under full decoupling the growth pays for wires, not profit.
The gradual loss of a battery's usable capacity with cycling and age. Storage contracts manage it with capacity guarantees and planned augmentation.

The part of a large customer's bill priced per kilowatt of peak demand rather than per kilowatt-hour of energy used. It pays for the wires and plant that have to exist to serve the customer's maximum draw, whether or not that draw occurs often — which is why a data center's bill is mostly demand, not energy.

A program that pays a customer to cut its grid draw when the system is stressed — by shedding load or by switching to on-site generation. Running backup engines for it moves them out of the emergency-only class, which is why the permit, not the machine, decides whether a data center can join.

Operating equipment below its nameplate rating because real conditions — ambient temperature, altitude, state of charge, or age — do not match the conditions the rating assumed. A specification read as a guaranteed operating number rather than a rated one is one of the most common sources of a capacity shortfall that presents as an equipment fault.

Being selected as the supplier for a component in a product that is about to be built — decided during the customer's design phase, often years before volume revenue. Once designed in, a part is expensive to replace, so the win locks in the socket for that product's life.

A simulated copy of a real asset, fed by its live data, used to rehearse changes before they touch the hardware — testing a control strategy, forecasting degradation, or learning what normal looks like so anomalies stand out. It is how an operator tries something on a plant without trying it on the plant.

Generation that can be turned on, up, down or off when the grid operator asks — gas, nuclear, hydro, and storage for as long as its energy lasts — as opposed to output that follows the weather. A plan that must serve a data center's flat load at night still buys dispatchable capacity, which is why gas keeps appearing in resource plans written under clean-energy mandates.

UPS topologies that reach N+1 or better without doubling everything. In a block-redundant or catcher design a spare UPS system stands ready to take any block's load through static transfer switches; in a distributed-redundant design each load is fed from two of several systems so any one can fail. Both cost less than 2N, and both place the redundancy in a switching event that has to work.

A commission's case file: a numbered proceeding holding the application, testimony, discovery, intervenor filings, hearing transcripts and the final order. For a seller the docket is the only place a utility's plans are stated under oath with dates attached — read the docket, not the press release.

The UPS mode in which all power is rectified to DC and re-made as AC by the inverter, continuously, so the load always sees a synthesized waveform and never the raw supply. It is the highest grade of protection — VFI in the IEC classification — and costs a few percent of every megawatt-hour as conversion heat; eco-mode is the alternative that idles the conversion and accepts a transfer.

A governor setting that lets an engine's speed fall slightly as its load rises, so several engines sharing a bus each take a predictable share of the load instead of fighting over it. Its partner is isochronous control, which holds speed exactly constant and is given to one machine or to the paralleling controller so the bus frequency stays put.

Diesel rotary uninterruptible power supply: a rotary UPS whose flywheel and synchronous machine share a shaft line with a diesel engine through a clutch. When the supply fails the flywheel carries the load for the seconds the engine needs to start and clutch in, so one machine does the work of UPS, transfer switch and generator — with no battery and no separate transfer.
How long a storage plant can discharge at full power (energy divided by power, MWh ÷ MW). Duration decides which grid jobs a battery can do — most US grid-scale projects run a few hours.

Running a static UPS with the load on the raw supply through the bypass and the conversion stage idling in reserve, lifting efficiency toward 98–99 percent. The bet is that the unit can detect a supply failure and transfer back to the inverter inside the servers' hold-up time, for every kind of fault — which is exactly what the mode's critics doubt.

Effective load carrying capability: how much of a resource's nameplate a grid operator counts toward meeting peak — its accredited capacity. A four-hour battery or a solar farm is credited well below nameplate and a gas plant close to it, so accreditation decides how many megawatts of storage a utility must build to satisfy a reserve requirement and how much a battery earns in a capacity market.

A public utility commission whose members are chosen by voters rather than appointed by a governor. Its decisions on rates and plants carry directly into election campaigns, so affordability politics reach the docket faster than in an appointed state — and a single election can change who decides the next case.

Colorado's name for the integrated resource plan: a two-phase docket in which the commission first approves the need and the resource envelope, then a competitive solicitation is run and the commission selects the winning bids from the utility's shortlist in a second decision. Phase two is where the developers, and therefore the equipment, are actually chosen.

Electric service agreement: the contract between a utility and one large customer that fixes the megawatts to be served, the term, the minimum bill, collateral and exit terms — the document that turns a request for load into an obligation the utility can finance a plant against.

The regulatory class for a stationary engine that runs only when the normal supply fails, plus a small annual allowance of hours for testing and maintenance. The class is what lets a backup fleet be permitted quickly and without the strictest emission controls — and it is lost the moment the same engines are run for prime power, peak shaving or a demand-response payment.

Energy management system: the supervisory software that decides when a storage plant charges and discharges — following price signals, grid instructions, or a contract — and coordinates the PCS and BMS to do it.

The moment new electrical infrastructure is first put under live voltage and proven, with the utility present. It is the line between contracted megawatts and connected ones: before it, a connection agreement is a promise; after it, power can actually flow, and every schedule upstream of it is measured against this date.

A battery optimized for how much it holds and how many times it can be emptied and refilled — sized by hours of duration and judged on cycle life and cost per stored unit. A grid storage container is the archetype, and it is the near-inverse of a power battery in almost every design choice.

The part of a bill priced per kilowatt-hour consumed — fuel and the variable cost of running plants. For a flat, always-on load it is large in total but it is the demand charge, not the energy charge, that decides whether the customer has paid for the capacity built to serve it.

A wholesale market design with no capacity market: generators are paid only for the energy they actually sell, and the incentive to build new plant comes from prices that spike when supply is scarce. ERCOT is the US example — no auction pays a plant to exist, so no commission certifies one, and whether a plant gets built is a private investment decision made against expected scarcity prices.
Engineering, procurement, and construction: the contractor model that delivers a plant turnkey under one contract — and the label for the firms that do it.

The share of a utility's regulatory capital structure funded by equity rather than debt. Regulators set it for ratemaking regardless of how the company actually finances itself. A higher equity ratio raises the allowed return in dollars, because equity earns the authorized return on equity while debt earns only its interest cost.

The Texas grid operator. An energy-only market with its own interconnection process — faster to connect, more volatile to operate in — which is why so much US storage and data-center buildout lands in Texas.

The DC current fed to a synchronous machine's rotor winding to create its magnetic field. Raising it lifts the output voltage and the reactive power the machine supplies; the automatic voltage regulator adjusts it continuously, and it is how a rotary UPS or a synchronous condenser holds voltage through a disturbance.

What a large customer owes if it leaves a utility contract before the term ends — typically the remaining minimum bills, or the unrecovered cost of the plant and wires built for it. With the term, the ramp and the credit support it is one of the four terms that make a data-center tariff financeable.

A power-chain design that splits the two jobs a converter normally does — holding the voltage steady (regulation) and changing its level (transformation) — into separate stages, so each can be built where it works best. The regulator lives upstream where the current is small, and a fixed-ratio current multiplier lives next to the load where the current is enormous.

The current that flows into a short circuit before a breaker clears it — many times the normal load current. A protection scheme needs enough of it to be sure the right breaker trips fast: a rotating machine delivers a large surge from its stored magnetic energy, while an inverter can supply only a little more than its rating, which changes how the downstream protection must be designed.

Foreign entity of concern: a US legal designation (tied to China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea) that disqualifies projects and products with too much such involvement from federal tax credits — a central bankability question for China-linked battery supply.

The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission: the US regulator of interstate transmission, wholesale power markets and the regional grid operators. State commissions set retail rates and certify plants; FERC sets the transmission tariff and approves the market rules and interconnection procedures the state-level story sits on top of.

How most interstate transmission is priced: a formula, approved by FERC, that turns the transmission owner's booked costs and rate base into an annual revenue requirement, updated every year without a contested case. It is the reason transmission is a utility's most predictable earnings line and why a regional plan award converts into earnings so smoothly.

Funds from operations: the cash a company generates from running its business before working-capital swings. Rating agencies judge a utility mainly on FFO as a percentage of its debt, so a large capital plan financed with borrowing pushes that ratio down — and a utility whose ratio approaches the agency's stated downgrade threshold has to raise equity, sell an asset or slow the plan.

The grid operator's last resort: ordering utilities to cut power to ordinary customers because supply cannot meet demand. Texas's 2025 large-load law ties the biggest customers to it — during an emergency the operator may direct a large load to run its backup generation or curtail before, or instead of, cutting homes.

Energy stored as rotation — half the moment of inertia times speed squared — in a heavy rotor or a fast light one on low-friction bearings, sometimes in a vacuum. It gives very high power for seconds, essentially unlimited cycles and no chemical aging, and its state of charge is simply its speed. In a UPS it covers a generator start; as a battery for hours it is the wrong tool.

A rate mechanism that resets a utility's rates every year by formula — actual earned return compared with an allowed band, with automatic adjustment — instead of a full contested rate case every few years. It cuts regulatory lag for the utility and gives the commission a yearly look at earnings; Entergy's Louisiana, Arkansas and Mississippi companies run on one.

Equipment that turns power at one frequency into power at another — 50 Hz to 60 Hz between grids and ships, or grid power to the 400 Hz that aircraft systems use on the ground. Rotary versions do it with a motor-generator, static versions with a rectifier and an inverter.

A resource that interconnects on the utility's side of the customer meter, like a small power plant, and is paid by wholesale markets or by contract — as opposed to behind-the-meter equipment on a customer's own site. Which side of the meter a project sits on decides the buyer, the contract, the rulebook, and the length of the sales cycle, which is why it is usually the first qualifying question asked.

Fixed Resource Requirement: PJM's alternative to bidding into the capacity auction, under which a utility commits to carry enough of its own accredited capacity to cover its load plus a reserve margin. It exempts that load from the auction's clearing price in both directions — no windfall when the price spikes, no relief when it collapses — and it is why two utilities in the same RTO can experience the same auction very differently.

The bill line that passes a utility's fuel and purchased-power costs straight through to customers, usually reset monthly or yearly with a true-up, and earning the utility no return. It is why gas prices show up on a bill within months while a new plant shows up only after a rate order.

An electrical barrier — usually a transformer — that lets power cross from one circuit to another with no conducting path between them, so a fault on one side cannot reach people or equipment on the other. A non-isolated converter drops the barrier for simplicity and density where the chain already provides one upstream.
Gallium nitride: a wide-bandgap semiconductor suited to very fast, compact low-to-mid-voltage converters — one of the two key materials (with SiC) shrinking modern power electronics.

Generator set: an engine or turbine coupled to an alternator on one frame, with its controls, cooling and fuel system — the packaged unit a data center buys, rather than a bare engine. Rated in kilowatts or kilovolt-amperes at a declared duty: standby, prime or continuous.

Grain-oriented electrical steel: the specialty magnetic steel every transformer core requires. Only a handful of mills worldwide produce it, and every announced transformer plant bids for the same tonnage — which is why transformer lead times, not capital, gate so many projects.

An inverter that locks onto the grid's existing voltage wave and injects current into it — a surfer riding a wave someone else is making. It is the conventional mode and works well, but it cannot operate at all without a live grid to follow, so it contributes nothing during the outage it is standing beside.
An inverter that sets its own voltage and frequency like a traditional generator, rather than following the grid's. It lets storage stabilize weak grids and restart dead ones (black start).

Distortion added to a clean AC waveform by loads that draw current in gulps rather than smoothly — rectifiers, drives, server power supplies. Harmonics overheat transformers and neutral conductors, nuisance-trip breakers, and distort the voltage other equipment sees; total harmonic distortion (THD) is the score, and under 5% is the common target.

The efficiency yardstick for a thermal power plant: fuel energy in per unit of electricity out, so a lower number is better. It decides which plants a market dispatches first, hour by hour, and it is the same quantity as percentage efficiency quoted the other way up.

The transmission tier — roughly 100 kV and up in the United States, with 230 kV, 500 kV and 765 kV the workhorse classes — used to move bulk power between regions and into a cluster of substations. Higher voltage carries more power over the same right-of-way with less loss, which is why the lines proposed for data-center corridors keep going up a class.

How long a server power supply can carry its load on internal capacitors after its input disappears — roughly 10 to 20 milliseconds. It is the physics referee for every power transfer: a switchover completed inside that window is invisible to the IT load, and one that misses it is an outage.

A parent corporation that owns several regulated operating utilities, each with its own territory, commission and rate base. Investors buy the parent; regulators regulate the subsidiaries — so one earnings call can describe five different regulatory relationships at once.

Removing or inserting a unit — a power supply, a converter shelf, a drive — while the rest of the system stays live. It works only because the unit and its slot were engineered for it: the connector sequence, the inrush control and the isolation of a failed unit are all deliberate design work.

High-voltage direct current: moving power as DC instead of AC — over long transmission links, and now inside the data center as the 800 VDC rack architecture. Fewer conversion stages and far less copper, at the cost of protection that cannot wait for an AC waveform to cross zero and extinguish the arc for it.
One of the giant cloud and platform operators that build and lease data-center capacity at gigawatt scale. Their capital spending sets the pace of the AI data-center buildout.

The heat made by current flowing through resistance: power lost equals current squared times resistance. Doubling the current through the same conductor quadruples the loss, which is why every power chain climbs to a higher voltage — and a lower current — for the long stretch and converts down only at the end.

Inverter-based resource: anything that reaches the grid through power electronics rather than through a spinning machine — solar, wind, and battery storage. The category exists because inverters behave differently from generators during a disturbance, so the reliability rules written for them are separate rules.

The international standard that classifies a UPS by how much of the supply's misbehavior reaches the load: VFD (voltage and frequency dependent — the supply passes through until it fails), VI (voltage independent — line-interactive, voltage corrected), and VFI (voltage and frequency independent — the load is fully isolated, as in double conversion or a rotary machine). Codes such as VFI-SS-111 add the output-waveform and transient grades so two makers' promises can be compared.

The standard that sets harmonic-distortion limits at the point of common coupling — the property line where a facility's electrical system meets the utility. It draws the boundary so one customer's distorted loads cannot degrade a neighbor's power quality, and compliance is measured at that point rather than assumed.

Insulated-gate bipolar transistor: the silicon switch that static UPS inverters, drives and grid inverters have been built on for three decades — fast enough to chop DC into a clean sine wave thousands of times a second and rugged enough for megawatts. Silicon carbide is displacing it where the last points of efficiency matter.

The technical diligence firm lenders hire to review a project on their behalf — the design, the equipment, the contracts, the production estimate. Its report is the gate to financial close, which makes the independent engineer, not the buyer, the audience a supplier's certifications and track record ultimately have to satisfy.

The stabilizing effect of heavy spinning generator masses, which resist sudden changes in grid frequency and buy operators seconds to react. As synchronous plants retire in favor of inverter-connected wind, solar, and storage, that inertia has to be replaced — by synchronous condensers, or by grid-forming inverters imitating it electronically.

The brief surge of current a device draws at the instant it is connected, as its empty capacitors charge in a rush. Uncontrolled, it can sag a shared bus, trip protection or pit a connector; precharge circuits exist to tame it.
The waiting line for grid-connection studies and approval. Multi-year queues are one of the main bottlenecks for new data centers and storage plants.

The voltage a rack or a server distributes between its main supply and the point-of-load converters — 12 volts in the older chain, 48 volts (often run at 54) in the modern one. Choosing it is a trade between the current the bus must carry, the safety rules it falls under, and how hard the final conversion becomes.

A tariff under which a large customer accepts that the utility may curtail its supply on short notice a set number of hours a year, in exchange for a lower rate. It lets the utility count on shedding that load at the system peak, which reduces the capacity it must build to serve everyone else.

A party admitted to a regulatory proceeding to represent an interest other than the utility's: consumer advocates, large industrial customers, environmental groups, municipalities, the commission's own staff. Intervenors file testimony proposing adjustments to the utility's request, and the gap between the filed request and the intervenors' recommendations frames what the commission ultimately decides.

A converter that turns direct current into alternating current — the mirror image of a rectifier. It appears wherever DC has to be handed back to an AC world: on the output of a battery or solar array, inside a UPS, and between an electric vehicle's pack and its motor. A bidirectional one that does both jobs is a power conversion system.

Earning revenue by letting other companies use patented technology under a royalty or fee instead of, or as well as, selling products. For a hardware company it turns a patent portfolio into a second business — and a lawsuit into a negotiation.

Integrated resource plan: a regulated utility's commission-filed roadmap of what it expects to need and how it intends to procure it. Certified IRP megawatts are the real demand pipeline for an equipment supplier — they become purchase orders on a multi-year fuse.

Running electrically disconnected from the grid, with on-site generation alone matching the load every second. There is no larger system to lean on, so frequency and voltage become the site's own problem — and so does restarting after a total loss.

The international standard that defines how reciprocating gen-sets are rated, so a kilowatt from one maker means the same as a kilowatt from another. Its rating classes — emergency standby, limited-time, prime and continuous — differ in the hours a year the set may run and the average load it may carry, not in the hardware.

A UPS topology in which many units are joined in a ring through chokes: in normal operation each unit feeds its own load, and when one fails its load is picked up by all the others sharing through the ring rather than by one dedicated spare. It reaches N+1 with one spare across a very large block instead of doubling the plant, and it is the shape in which rotary UPS is sold at tens of megawatts.
The US investment tax credit: a percentage of a storage or solar project's cost returned as a federal tax credit. A core driver of BESS project economics, with bonus tiers for domestic content.

SPP's Integrated Transmission Plan: the yearly planning process in which the grid operator identifies the lines the plains grid needs, approves a portfolio and assigns projects to transmission owners, with cost allocation across the region. Its 2024 and 2025 portfolios were the largest in the operator's history and included the first 765 kV lines in its footprint.

The policy of retiring coal plants on a schedule while funding the workers and communities that depended on them. Colorado wrote it into law in 2019 with a 2030 carbon target and a state office; it is why the state's resource plans pair a coal retirement date with a replacement build and a community package in the same decision.

The shorthand for a provision in Texas's 2025 large-load law: the grid operator can require a very large customer to install equipment that lets the operator curtail it remotely during a firm load-shed emergency. In practice it is a curtailment protocol with the operator, not the customer, holding the switch.

The process by which a very large new customer — a data center, a hydrogen plant, a crypto mine — is studied and connected to the transmission system. In ERCOT the wires utility runs the studies and builds the substation, the grid operator reviews the request against the wider system, and since 2025 the state's rules set fees, security and curtailment terms for it. It is a load process, distinct from the generator interconnection queue.

A utility rate class written specifically for very large customers such as data centers: long contract terms, minimum-take obligations, exit fees, and collateral. It is the filter that separates real demand from speculative interconnection requests, and the instrument that turns AI load into something a utility can plan and finance against.

Feeding a processor from converters mounted on the board beside the package, with the current running sideways through the board's copper for the last centimetre. It is the conventional arrangement, and the one that runs out of room and out of copper as chip currents climb.

A gas-engine combustion strategy that burns with excess air, which lowers peak flame temperature and so forms far less nitrogen oxide inside the cylinder. It is how a natural-gas gen-set meets a tight air permit with little after-treatment, at the cost of a slower response to sudden load steps than a diesel.

Lithium iron phosphate: a lithium-ion battery chemistry using an iron-phosphate cathode. It trades some energy density for lower cost, longer cycle life, and much better thermal stability than nickel-based chemistries — which is why it dominates grid-scale storage.

Average demand divided by peak demand over a period. A data center running at 90 percent or more is the flattest load a utility serves; a house at 30 percent peaks for a few hours a day. Flat loads use the wires and plants built for them almost all the time, which is why tariffs single them out.

The projection of future peak demand and energy that a utility's plan and a grid operator's markets are built on. Data-center requests inflated these forecasts faster than anything in the industry's history, and the arguments — how much of the queue is real, whether the same campus is counted by several utilities — are arguments about this number.

Dropping pre-ranked non-critical loads — chillers, offices, lower-priority halls — when generation cannot carry everything, so the critical load keeps its power. The priority list is written in advance and executed automatically by the paralleling controls; it is the reason an under-strength generator fleet degrades gracefully instead of tripping.

A sudden change in the current a load draws — a processor jumping from idle to full work in microseconds. The converter must hold the voltage through it, and how fast it responds, and how much stored charge sits beside the chip to cover the gap, is a central design constraint.

Storage that can discharge for ten hours or more — iron-air, flow batteries, pumped hydro — as opposed to the two- to four-hour lithium-ion plants that make up nearly all of today's grid storage. It targets multi-day gaps in wind and solar rather than the evening peak, and it is still mostly at pilot scale.

Utilization-level voltage — under about a thousand volts, the 400 or 480 V that feeds distribution boards, UPS units and the racks. Most UPS equipment has historically lived here; moving it up to medium voltage is one of the live arguments in gigawatt campuses.

Long-term service agreement: the multi-year operations-and-maintenance contract through which a supplier delivers availability guarantees on the equipment it sold. Suppliers generally will not extend long-dated warranties without holding it, so the LTSA and the warranty are negotiated as one package.

A bearing that holds a shaft in place with controlled magnetic fields instead of contact, so a high-speed flywheel can spin with almost no friction and no lubrication. It is what lets a small, light rotor store useful energy at tens of thousands of rpm — and it needs control power of its own.

An air-permitting classification for a plant whose potential emissions exceed the thresholds that trigger full pre-construction review — modelling, public comment and best-available-control analysis. Crossing the line turns a permit measured in months into one measured in years, so on-site plants are packaged to stay under it.
Distribution-level voltage, roughly the single-digit to tens of kilovolts — the tier data centers and storage plants connect at before power is stepped down to usable levels.

A self-contained power system — generation, storage, and controls — that can run connected to the grid or islanded on its own. It is how some AI campuses get power before utility interconnection arrives.

A tariff term that bills a large customer for a fixed share of its contracted capacity every month whether or not it draws it — the utility's version of take-or-pay. It converts a speculative interconnection request into demand the utility can finance plant against, and it is what makes a phased campus pay for megawatts it has not energized yet.

An air-permitting category for a plant whose potential emissions sit below the major-source thresholds, sometimes by accepting enforceable limits on hours or fuel — a synthetic minor. It replaces months of modelling and public comment with a far lighter permit, which is why on-site power blocks are sized to fit beneath the line.

The share of a subsidiary's earnings that belongs to an outside investor rather than to the parent's shareholders. Selling a minority stake raises cash without issuing shares, and the price is a permanent deduction from reported earnings — which is why a utility's earnings can fall in a year its business grew.

The Midcontinent Independent System Operator — the RTO for fifteen central US states and Manitoba. Its South region, added in 2013, covers Louisiana, Arkansas, Mississippi and the Texas Gulf coast, so Entergy's operating companies buy and sell wholesale power, get their capacity accredited and have their big lines planned there rather than in ERCOT or PJM.

Mean time between failures: the average running time between one failure and the next across a population of a device, calculated from its parts count or from field data. It is a statement about a fleet rather than a promise about one unit, and it says nothing about how long the repair takes — which is why availability also needs the mean time to repair.

The MISO Transmission Expansion Plan — the RTO's yearly regional transmission plan, the MISO counterpart of PJM's RTEP. Big lines are approved here and their cost allocated across the footprint, on a horizon of five to fifteen years.

A rate case that sets rates for several years at once, with pre-approved step increases as a capital plan is built, instead of a new case each time. It gives the utility certainty on recovery and the commission a settled bill trajectory; Minnesota and Colorado use it, and it is the instrument through which a large capital plan lands on customers on a schedule.

Redundancy shorthand: N is the equipment needed to carry the load, N+1 adds one spare unit, 2N doubles everything. Data centers price reliability in these terms — more redundancy means fewer outages and more capital.

The maximum output a generator is rated to produce under ideal conditions, stamped on the machine. It is not what the resource contributes to meeting peak demand: a 100 MW nameplate solar farm may be credited with a fraction of that in a planning study. Portfolio announcements are usually stated in nameplate, and accredited or effective capacity is the smaller number that actually counts.

A US defense-authorization provision restricting Department of Defense battery procurement from named Chinese suppliers — the list that made "is your cell maker §154-listed?" a standard sourcing question.
A newer GPU-cloud provider renting AI compute capacity, typically growing faster than its capital base — a distinct buyer class from the hyperscalers.

The US standard for emergency and standby power systems. It classes a system by how fast it must pick up the load after the normal supply fails — the usual data-center class must be carrying load within ten seconds — and by how long it must be able to run, and it sets the testing and maintenance regime that keeps a backup plant honest.
The US fire-protection standard for stationary energy storage installations — spacing, enclosures, suppression, and the fire testing (UL 9540A) it references. Permitting officials work from it.

Nickel manganese cobalt: a lithium-ion cathode chemistry with higher energy density than LFP but higher cost and more thermal-runaway risk — favored where weight matters, largely displaced by LFP in stationary storage.

The ERCOT rule change setting ride-through obligations for inverter-based resources, battery storage included. It is the resource-side counterpart to NOGRR 282, which governs large electronic loads: adjacent numbers, opposite sides of the same interface, and confusing the two is a common and expensive error in a technical room.

The ERCOT rule requiring new large electronic loads — data centers of 75 MW and up — to ride through voltage and frequency disturbances instead of tripping off together. It is a load rule rather than a storage standard (those are NOGRR 245 and 272), and it is what makes buffering between the grid and the GPUs close to mandatory in Texas.

A region where outdoor air already fails a federal ambient standard for a pollutant such as ozone or fine particulates. Adding a combustion source there faces the strictest review and offset requirements, so low-emission machines can site where diesel and open-flame plants cannot.

Nitrogen oxides: the pollutant family formed when the air's own nitrogen burns at high flame temperature. It drives ozone formation downwind and is the number most air permits are written around — which is why diesels carry after-treatment, gas engines run lean and turbines carry low-NOx combustors.

Raising an existing reactor's licensed output — by a few percent through better instrumentation, or by up to a fifth through new turbines and equipment — with the regulator's approval. It is the cheapest firm capacity a utility with a nuclear fleet can add, because the site, the licence and the operators already exist.
The committed purchase of a project's output — power, capacity, or storage services. Signed offtake is what turns a development pipeline into a financeable project.

A transfer that opens the old source before closing onto the new one — break-before-make — so for a moment the load is fed by nothing. Simpler, and it never back-feeds the utility, but the gap means the UPS or some other stored energy has to carry the load across it or the servers see an outage.

Joining two or more sources to one bus through devices that let current flow only out of each source — an OR gate for power. A source that fails or is unplugged cannot drag the bus down or draw current from its neighbours, which is what makes redundant supplies and live swaps safe.

Switchgear whose controller synchronizes several generators onto one common bus, adds them in a set order, shares the load between them and sheds low-priority load if generation runs short — a room of engines behaving as one plant. It is what turns a collection of standby gen-sets into a campus-scale power source.

Running a generating machine below its full rating. Efficiency and emissions both move with load — a large gas turbine is efficient only near full output, while a fleet of engines can shut units down and keep the rest at their sweet spot — so the shape of the load, not just its peak, decides which machine is cheaper to run.

Power conversion system: the bidirectional inverter of a battery plant — converts the batteries' DC to grid AC when discharging and back when charging. Its rating sets the plant's power (MW), while the batteries set its energy (MWh).

Power delivery network: everything between a converter's output and the transistors on the chip — board copper, package pins, vias, the substrate and the decoupling capacitors along the way. Its resistance and inductance set how much voltage is lost on the way and how fast the supply can answer a transient.
Power distribution unit: data-center gear that splits and distributes power to the racks — the branch circuits between the UPS and the servers.

The largest US regional grid operator, spanning the mid-Atlantic and parts of the Midwest — including northern Virginia's data-center corridor. Its capacity market and interconnection queue shape much of the AI data-center power story.

The cushion of accredited capacity a system must hold above its forecast peak — typically 15 to 25 percent — so that outages, weather and forecast error do not produce shortfalls. A rising load forecast raises the megawatts the margin requires; the margin, not the peak, is what a utility certifies plants against.

The final converter in the chain, placed as close as physically possible to the device it feeds, so that the very large current at a very low voltage travels only millimetres. Everything upstream can run at a higher voltage; the point of load is where the chain gives that up.

A transmission charge spread evenly across every customer in a region regardless of where the line was built — the same price to send a letter anywhere. ERCOT allocates its transmission cost of service this way across all load, which is why a 765 kV line in West Texas is paid for by customers in Dallas and Houston, and why Texas has built transmission faster than regions that argue about who benefits.

A battery optimized for how fast it can deliver rather than how much it holds — sized by discharge rate against a short duration, and judged on rate capability and on how well it survives sitting fully charged. A backup-supply battery is the archetype, and its design choices run opposite to an energy battery's at almost every point.

Cleaning up the supply before it reaches the load — holding voltage and frequency steady, removing harmonics, riding through sags and spikes — as distinct from replacing the supply when it fails. Every UPS does some of it; a double-conversion or rotary unit does all of it, all the time.

How much conversion capability fits in a given volume, usually watts per cubic inch or per litre. In racks where every rack unit is contested, a denser converter buys back space for compute — which is why the metric has become a competitive scoreboard.

The ratio of useful power to apparent power — how much of the current a facility draws actually does work. The rest is reactive power: magnetizing current sloshing between source and load, doing nothing but occupying wires and transformers, which is why utilities bill penalties when it runs low.

A slide-in conversion tray occupying rack units and feeding the rack's own DC busbar, replacing per-server conversion with a pooled stage. Shelves are built with one more module than the load needs, so any single module can fail or be swapped while the rack keeps running.
Power purchase agreement: a long-term contract to buy a project's power or capacity at agreed terms — the bankable revenue stream that lets developers finance construction.

MISO's Planning Resource Auction — the yearly auction that clears capacity for the coming year, by season and by zone, and sets the price a utility short of its reserve margin pays. MISO's counterpart of PJM's Base Residual Auction, with a one-year rather than three-year horizon.

The North American reliability standard making ride-through mandatory for inverter-based resources, storage included — the continent-wide counterpart to what individual grid operators had already required regionally. It is the point at which ride-through capability stops being a regional differentiator and becomes a baseline everywhere.

A circuit that charges a unit's capacitors gently through a resistor or a controlled switch before the main connection closes, so a live insertion does not draw a damaging inrush surge. It is the quiet engineering that makes hot-swap possible.

Generation that carries a site's full load continuously, as its main source — the opposite of standby plant that sits idle until the normal supply fails. The distinction changes the machine, the air permit, and the maintenance regime, so a plant sold as prime and a plant sold as backup are different products even when the hardware looks alike.

ERCOT's term for a site with its own generation and load behind one point of connection to the grid — an industrial plant or a data-center campus that generates part of what it consumes. Its net position is what the grid sees; the rules on what such a site owes for the grid it leans on are the co-location argument in Texas form.

The commission's after-the-fact test of whether a utility's spending was reasonable when the decision was made; imprudent cost is disallowed and falls on shareholders instead of customers. It is the reason a regulated buyer cares so much about a supplier's bankability and paperwork: every purchase must survive this review years later.

Public safety power shutoff: deliberately de-energizing lines in high-risk areas during extreme wind and dry conditions so that a fallen wire cannot start a fire. It trades certain outages for uncertain fires, and a utility is criticized for calling one and sued for not calling one.

A US federal tax credit paid per megawatt-hour generated over a project's first ten years, historically the principal support for wind. Unlike an investment credit, which rewards capital spent, it rewards output, so it favours high-capacity-factor resources. The 2025 budget law ends it for wind and solar placed in service after 2027 where construction begins after July 4, 2026.

The state body that regulates a monopoly utility: it approves rates, certifies new plants and lines, reviews the integrated resource plan and decides what the utility may recover from customers. Called a PUC, a PSC or, in Virginia, the State Corporation Commission — whatever the name, nothing a regulated utility buys at scale is final until it has been through this body.

Power usage effectiveness: total facility power divided by the power that reaches the IT equipment. A PUE of 1.0 would mean every watt went to computing; the gap above it is cooling, conversion, and lighting overhead — the industry's headline efficiency number.

Pulse-width modulation: controlling a converter by switching fully on and fully off at a fixed rate and varying only the fraction of each cycle spent on — the duty cycle. A switch that is either fully on or fully off wastes little, which is the basic reason switching converters beat the old linear ones.

The years a large-load tariff gives a new customer to grow into its contracted demand before the minimum bill applies in full — a schedule such as forty percent in year one, sixty in year two, then the whole contract demand. It recognizes that a campus energizes in halls, and it is the term a developer negotiates hardest after the term itself.

The value of a regulated utility's plant in service — generation, wires, substations, meters — net of depreciation, on which the commission lets it earn a return. Every dollar of prudently built plant that goes into rate base earns the allowed return for decades, which is why a regulated utility's growth story is a capital-spending story and why it would rather own an asset than contract for one.

The commission proceeding in which a utility's base rates are reset: the utility files its costs and rate base, intervenors test them, and an order sets the revenue requirement, the allowed return and the rate classes for the years ahead. Virginia runs Dominion Energy Virginia's as a biennial review. It is the moment a large-load tariff can be created or rewritten.

A group of customers billed under the same tariff schedule — residential, small commercial, large industrial, and now very large loads — because they cost the utility different amounts to serve. Creating a rate class is how a commission fences a data center's costs off from everyone else's bill.

An agreement or order holding a utility's base rates flat for a set period, usually in exchange for something — a settled case, deferred costs, a political truce before an election. Costs still accrue; the freeze decides when customers pay them, not whether.
A power-electronics device that turns AC into DC — the first stage of nearly every power supply, charger, and data-center power shelf.

A cost a utility has incurred but not yet recovered, which the commission has agreed may be collected from customers in the future. It sits on the balance sheet as an asset because a regulator's promise of recovery has value. Deferring costs into a regulatory asset lets a utility spend ahead of a rate case, at the price of a later prudence review that can disallow the deferral.

The gap between when a utility spends money and when a rate order lets it recover that money. Long lag erodes the earned return below the allowed one; riders, formula rate plans and CWIP recovery all exist to shorten it.

A restructured market in which the wires company delivers power but customers buy the energy from competing retailers, and generation is not in rate base. Most of Texas works this way inside ERCOT; the Southeast and MISO South do not, which is why a data center there signs with one integrated utility rather than a retailer and a wires company.

The total a utility is allowed to collect from customers over a period: operating costs plus depreciation plus taxes plus the allowed return on rate base. A rate case is an argument about this one number, and the tariffs are how it is divided among customer classes.

Request for proposals: the competitive solicitation a utility issues for the capacity its plan calls for — a storage-specific, solar or all-source RFP — evaluated by the utility or an independent evaluator and then taken to the commission for approval. For an equipment vendor it is the moment the bidding developer's bill of materials locks, which is earlier than the award.

Staying connected and operating through a grid disturbance — a voltage dip or a frequency excursion — instead of protectively disconnecting. Grid codes increasingly require it of both resources and very large loads, for a blunt reason: if everything connected trips at the first sign of trouble, a local fault becomes a system-wide one.

A separate line on the bill that recovers one program's cost outside the base rates — a new plant, a transmission program, offshore wind, fuel. Riders let a utility start earning on a project without waiting for the next rate case, which is why regulators guard them and why a utility's biggest projects each tend to arrive with one.

A UPS built around a rotating synchronous machine rather than power electronics: the machine, fed through a choke, generates a clean sine wave for the load, and a flywheel on its shaft supplies the energy when the input fails. It has no battery, delivers a large fault current, isolates the load from harmonics on the supply and connects readily at medium voltage; its costs are bearings, maintenance and a few points of efficiency.

The share of energy put into a storage system that comes back out after conversion and thermal losses — typically in the high-80s percent range for lithium-ion. The gap is energy bought but never sold.

PJM's Regional Transmission Expansion Plan: the annual process in which the grid operator identifies reliability needs, opens competitive windows and assigns transmission projects — with their cost allocation — to utilities and developers. The billion-dollar lines into a data-center cluster are chosen here, years before they are built.

Regional transmission organization: the FERC-regulated operator that runs the wholesale markets, the interconnection queue and the regional transmission plan across many utilities — PJM, MISO, SPP. A regulated utility inside one still owns its wires and plants, but the price of capacity and the plan for the big lines are set at the RTO, one level above its own commission.

Starting a project far enough — by spending, or by taking delivery of equipment — to lock in the tax rules in force at that moment, even if those rules later change. It creates a cohort of owners still buying under older terms, and therefore a procurement channel whose constraints differ from everyone else's.

The 2025 Texas law setting the terms on which very large loads connect to the grid: screening-study fees and proof of site control up front, mandatory curtailment protocols, and disclosure of on-site backup generation. It is the template other states are copying, and it is what makes a data center's ability to shed or buffer load a condition of connecting at all.

Supervisory control and data acquisition: the operator's window onto a plant — live telemetry out, remote commands in. It is a visibility and intervention layer rather than a deciding one; the automated control loops below it are acting far faster than anyone is watching.

The two ways AI machines are wired together. Scale-up is the memory-speed link that makes a group of GPUs behave as one accelerator — it rides copper, so its reach is about one rack. Scale-out is the switched network between racks, with longer latency and protocol overhead, which is why so much engineering effort goes into packing more compute and more power into that single rack-sized domain.

Virginia's State Corporation Commission — the state's public utility commission, a three-judge body that sets Dominion Energy Virginia's rates in biennial reviews, certifies its plants and lines, reviews its integrated resource plan and approved its large-load rate class. Its dockets are the primary record of how Data Center Alley gets its power.
US tariffs on Chinese imports imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act — including steep rates on lithium-ion batteries — that reshape the landed cost of China-sourced storage hardware.

The U.S. trade statute under which the International Trade Commission investigates imported products accused of infringing a U.S. patent. Its remedy is not damages but an exclusion order — the product is stopped at the border — which makes it a fast and heavy lever in hardware patent disputes.

Financing a specific approved cost — storm damage, a retired plant — by selling bonds backed by a dedicated charge on customer bills, so the utility recovers the money at once at a low interest rate instead of carrying it in rate base for years. Common after Gulf hurricanes.

The Southeast Energy Exchange Market — a bilateral, fifteen-minute trading platform among Southeastern utilities that are not in any RTO. It is not a market operator: there is no central dispatch, no capacity auction and no queue; each utility remains its own balancing authority.

Exhaust after-treatment that injects a urea or ammonia solution across a catalyst to convert nitrogen oxides into nitrogen and water. It is the standard control that lets a diesel or gas plant meet a tight air permit, and it is equipment, space and a consumable rather than a setting.

Arranging breakers in series so a fault trips only the nearest device upstream of it, cutting the failure away surgically while the rest of the building keeps running. Engineers nest the devices' time-current curves so the downstream breaker always wins the race; without it, a rack-level fault can open a main breaker and darken a whole hall.

A utility's proposal to build and own a plant itself, evaluated against third-party bids in an all-source solicitation. Because owned plant enters rate base and a contract does not, commissions watch whether the self-build was compared fairly with the bids.

Safety extra-low voltage: a supply below about 60 volts DC that the safety standards treat as safe to touch, so it can be handled, wired and serviced without the insulation, clearances and lockout that higher voltages demand. The 48-volt rack bus sits deliberately just under that line.

A negotiated resolution of a regulatory proceeding, signed by the utility and some or all intervening parties and submitted to the commission for approval. A settlement can be unopposed, meaning every party signed, or contested. Commissions are not bound by settlements and can modify or reject them, which is the difference between agreeing with your opponents and winning.

Silicon carbide: a wide-bandgap semiconductor that switches faster with lower losses than silicon, at higher voltages and temperatures — the material behind smaller, more efficient inverters and converters.

A conversion cabinet standing beside a rack that produces the rack's high-voltage DC bus from whatever the building already distributes. It is a bridge product by design: it delivers a new power architecture to one rack without rebuilding the hall around it — which is also the precise boundary of what it fixes, since the hall's upstream capacity is unchanged.

A gas turbine that drives a generator and vents its hot exhaust rather than recovering it. Cheaper, faster to build, and quick to start, but only roughly 35 to 40 percent of the fuel's energy reaches the wires — which is why it survives as a peaking and bridge machine rather than as baseload.

A fixed-ratio converter that drives its transformer with a pure sine-wave current at resonance and switches its transistors only as that current passes through zero, so almost nothing is wasted in the switching itself. The idea lets a current multiplier run at very high frequency, which shrinks its magnetics and raises its density.

Small modular reactor: a nuclear plant designed as factory-built units of roughly 50 to 300 MW each rather than one gigawatt-class build, meant to be licensed once and repeated. None is yet operating commercially in the United States; for a utility and a hyperscaler the attraction is clean, dispatchable power on an existing nuclear site, and the constraint is a licensing and construction clock measured in a decade.
A battery chemistry replacing lithium with abundant sodium — cheaper materials and better cold-weather performance at lower energy density; an emerging challenger for stationary storage.

Switching a converter's transistors at the instant the voltage or current across them is zero, so the transition itself dissipates almost nothing. Hard switching — turning off while current still flows — wastes energy on every edge, which limits how fast a converter can switch and therefore how small it can be.

A fuel cell with a ceramic electrolyte that works only when very hot, roughly 700 to 1,000 degrees Celsius. The heat is the point: at that temperature natural gas breaks down into hydrogen right at the electrode, so the cell runs on pipeline gas rather than purified hydrogen. There is no flame, so nitrogen oxides and particulates are near zero — but the ceramics dislike being cycled and prefer steady output.

Generating units already running and synchronized but deliberately loaded below their capability, so their headroom is available in seconds rather than in the minutes a cold start would take. On an islanded campus it is the margin that absorbs a load swing or a unit trip without the frequency wandering.

Southwest Power Pool: the regional grid operator for the central US plains — Oklahoma, Kansas, the Texas Panhandle, Arkansas, Louisiana, the Dakotas and neighbours. Like PJM and MISO it runs the wholesale market, the interconnection queue and a regional transmission plan; it has a capacity requirement on its utilities rather than a centralized capacity auction.

Solid-state circuit breaker: a breaker that interrupts electronically in a fraction of a millisecond, before fault current reaches its peak, instead of physically parting contacts. It is the enabling protection device for DC distribution, where there is no AC zero crossing to help extinguish the arc.

Solid-state transformer: a power-electronics replacement for the iron transformer that converts medium-voltage AC directly to regulated DC using high-frequency switching — a candidate to collapse today's multi-stage data-center power chain into one device.

The generator rating for carrying a varying load only while the normal supply is out, for a limited number of hours a year and with no overload allowance. It is the highest kilowatt number the same engine will carry — and the one a data center's backup fleet is bought against, which is why a standby set cannot simply be re-labelled prime.

The fuel gauge: how much energy is on board right now, as a percentage of what the plant can hold. Operators run a narrower window than the physical one because cells age faster held near either extreme, and every dispatch decision is planned around this number.

The long-term gauge: how much capacity a battery still holds compared with when it was new. Where state of charge moves through the day, state of health only ever falls — and how fast it falls is what a capacity warranty is a promise about.

The path around a UPS's conversion stages that connects the load straight to the raw supply — automatically, through a solid-state static switch, when the UPS overloads or fails, or manually, through a maintenance bypass, so the unit can be serviced. While the load is on bypass it is unprotected: the stored seconds are not available.

A UPS built from power electronics — a rectifier, a DC link with batteries on it and an inverter — with no moving parts except fans. It is the incumbent form in data centers: modular, efficient, factory-built at low voltage, and dependent on a battery room whose chemistry, life and fire code are a design in themselves.

Investment a utility made to serve a customer or a market that then went away, leaving the plant unpaid for. The fear behind every large-load tariff term — minimum demand, long contracts, collateral, exit fees — is a substation and a gas plant built for a data center that never fully arrives, with the bill landing on everyone else.

A legal standard under which a party is liable for harm regardless of fault or negligence. In utility wildfire law it means a utility whose equipment ignited a fire pays even if it maintained the line reasonably. Some states apply it or the related doctrine of inverse condemnation; others require proof of negligence. Which standard a state uses is the single largest variable in a utility's wildfire exposure.

The fenced yard where transmission voltage is stepped down through large transformers and routed through switchgear onto distribution or onto a customer's own feeders. A data-center campus gets one — often several — and the transformer lead time, the land and the transmission line feeding it are what a utility means when it says it cannot connect a load before a given year.

The layered board a processor die is mounted on inside its package, carrying the die's thousands of connections out to the pins or balls beneath. It is where the power delivery network ends — and, increasingly, where the last converter is asked to sit.

A device storing energy as separated electric charge rather than as a chemical reaction. It holds far less energy than a battery of the same size but takes it in and gives it back within milliseconds, over and over, for many years — which makes it the right part for absorbing a spike and the wrong one for riding out an outage.
